title: Model Performance
summary: How to tell whether a model is any good. Cross-validation for honest estimates, the confusion matrix and everything derived from it, and the two curves — precision-recall and ROC — that describe a classifier across all thresholds rather than at one.

formulas.name: Precision
formulas.note: Of everything predicted positive, how much really was. Denominator is a column of the confusion matrix.

formulas.name: Recall
formulas.note: Of everything actually positive, how much was found. Denominator is a row of the confusion matrix.

subtopics.title: Training vs test error
subtopics.summary: Training error falls monotonically with complexity; test error turns back up. The distance between them is the generalization gap.

keyFacts.definition: The gap between the test error and the training error.

questions.prompt: What is the gap between test error and training error called?
Describe how training and test error behave as model complexity increases.
questions.answer:
**Training error** falls steadily — a more complex model can always fit the data it has seen better.

**Test error** falls at first, then **turns back up** past some point of complexity.

The region left of the turning point is **underfitting**; the region right of it is **overfitting**. The widening distance between the curves is the generalization gap.

questions.prompt: On the error-versus-complexity plot, the region to the **left** of the minimum test error is labelled:
Under what condition is validation error a good estimate of test accuracy?
options: When training and test data are drawn from the same distribution
When the validation set is at least half the data
Always — that is what validation is for
questions.explanation: The slide's own gloss: 'a fancy way of saying if the training data and the test data are similar'.

questions.prompt: Complete the phrase: the error on the validation set estimates test accuracy well if the data are drawn from the same ___.
A model scores {{tr}}% accuracy on the training set and {{te}}% on the test set. How large is the generalization gap, in percentage points?

steps.text: The gap is the difference between training and test performance.

questions.explanation: A large gap points to overfitting. A small gap at a poor absolute score points to underfitting instead.

questions.prompt: State the error decomposition and which parts can be traded off.
questions.answer:
`Generalization error = Bias + Variance + Irreducible error`

**Bias and variance** can be traded against each other by moving along the complexity axis. **Irreducible error** is noise and cannot be traded at all — it is the floor.

questions.prompt: According to the error decomposition slide, the most performant model on new data is the one with:
options: The best tradeoff between bias and variance
The most parameters that still converge

questions.prompt: In the c4 diagrams, what does Ē_new denote?
options: The expected error on new data
questions.explanation: It is plotted against Ē_train, and the vertical distance between them is the generalization gap.

questions.prompt: What other name does c4 give the validation set?
Training error is very low but test error is high. Diagnose it and give two remedies.
questions.answer:
**Overfitting** — a large generalization gap.

Remedies: **more training data**, or a **less complex / more constrained model** (fewer parameters, fewer features, stronger regularization).

questions.prompt: Training error and test error are both high and close together. What is the problem?
options: Underfitting — the model is too simple
Overfitting — the model memorised the data
The test set is too small
The learning rate is too high

questions.prompt: As the model becomes more complex, training error generally {{1}}, while at some point test error starts to {{2}}.
Why can training error never be used to choose model complexity?
questions.answer:
Because it **decreases monotonically** with complexity. Selecting on it would always pick the most complex model available — the most overfitted one.

The turning point that matters only exists on the **test or validation** curve, so selection must happen on held-out data.

subtopics.title: Cross-validation
subtopics.summary: An alternative to a single train/validation split: k folds, k fits, k results, then mean and standard deviation. It uses all the data for both purposes without ever testing on what it trained on.

keyFacts.definition: Split train into k equal-sized folds (default 10). Use k−1 together as the new train, validate on the remaining fold. Repeat k times, always choosing another fold, giving k results. Report mean + standard deviation.

questions.prompt: Describe k-fold cross-validation, including what is reported at the end.
questions.answer:
1. Split **train** into **k equal-sized folds** (default 10).
2. Use **k−1 folds** together as the new training set, validate on the **remaining fold**.
3. **Repeat k times**, each time holding out a different fold — giving k results.
4. Compute the **mean and standard deviation** of those k results.

It can be repeated with different random seeds to reduce the variance of the result further.

questions.prompt: What does c4 give as the default number of folds?
questions.explanation: Note the code examples use `cv=3`, which is a speed compromise on MNIST, not the stated default.

questions.prompt: Cross-validation is described as an alternative to what?
questions.explanation: The test set is still held out separately. Cross-validation replaces the *validation* split, not the test set.

questions.prompt: Why repeat cross-validation with different random seeds?
options: To further reduce the variance of the result
To increase the size of the training set
To avoid overfitting the test set

questions.prompt: A training set of {{k * per}} examples is split into {{k}} folds. How many examples are in each fold?

steps.text: The folds are equal-sized, so each holds `n / k` examples.

questions.prompt: A training set of {{k * per}} examples is split into {{k}} folds. In each round, how many examples are used for **training**?

steps.text: Each fold holds `{{n}} / {{k}} = {{per}}` examples, and one fold is held out to validate on.
So `k − 1 = {{k - 1}}` folds are used for training.

questions.prompt: You cross-validate {{m}} candidate models with {{k}}-fold cross-validation. How many model fits are performed in total?

steps.text: Each model is fitted once per fold, so k fits per model.

questions.explanation: This is why cross-validation is expensive, and why `cv=3` shows up in the MNIST examples instead of the stated default of 10.

questions.prompt: What does `cross_val_score(sgd_clf, X_train, y_train_5, cv=3, scoring="accuracy")` return?
options: An array of three accuracy scores, one per fold
The predictions for every training example
questions.explanation: The output shown is `array([0.9532, 0.95125, 0.9625])` — one score per fold.

questions.prompt: How does `cross_val_predict` differ from `cross_val_score`?
options: It returns the predictions themselves rather than scores
It fits on the test set instead of the train set
It uses a fixed split rather than folds
It returns probabilities rather than labels
questions.explanation: Every prediction comes from a model that did not see that example, which is what makes it safe to build a confusion matrix from.

questions.prompt: Which class does the long-form cross-validation example use?
questions.explanation: Stratified folds preserve the class balance in each fold, which matters when the positive class is rare — as it is in the 5-vs-rest MNIST task.

questions.prompt: In the long-form cross-validation code, why is `clone(sgd_clf)` called inside the loop?
questions.answer:
To get a **fresh, unfitted copy** of the classifier for each fold.

Without it, each iteration would continue training the same fitted object, so later folds would be evaluated by a model that had already seen their data — destroying the independence cross-validation exists to provide.

questions.prompt: How is the MNIST dataset described in c4?
options: 50000 + 10000 grey-scale 28×28 noisy images of digits 0 to 9

questions.prompt: Give the main advantage and the main cost of cross-validation over a single hold-out split.
questions.answer:
**Advantage:** every example is used for both training and validation across the rounds, so the estimate uses all the data and comes with a **standard deviation** as well as a mean — you learn how stable the result is.

**Cost:** k times the computation, since the model is fitted k times instead of once.

questions.prompt: After k rounds, cross-validation reports the {{1}} and the {{2}} of the k results.
Why is cross-validation run on the training data rather than the whole dataset?
questions.answer:
Because the **test set must stay untouched** until the very end. Cross-validation is used for **model selection and hyperparameter tuning**, and anything used for selection stops being an honest estimate of final performance.

The recommended setup is: split into train + test, then cross-validate **within** train.

questions.prompt: What changes as k increases in k-fold cross-validation?
questions.answer:
Each round trains on **more data** (k−1 out of k folds), so each fitted model is closer to one trained on the full set — a **less pessimistic** estimate.

But there are **more rounds**, so the cost rises linearly with k, and each validation fold is smaller, making each individual score noisier.

subtopics.title: The confusion matrix
subtopics.summary: Rows are actual classes, columns are predictions. Getting that orientation right is what makes every derived metric come out correctly.

keyFacts.definition: **Rows** carry information about the actual class — row 0 is class 0. **Columns** carry information about the prediction — column 0 is predicted-as-0.

questions.prompt: What do the rows and columns of a confusion matrix represent?
questions.answer:
**Rows** — the **actual** class. Row 0 holds information about class 0.
**Columns** — the **predicted** class. Column 0 holds information about what was predicted as 0.

So the entry at [row i, column j] counts examples that really were class i and were predicted as class j.

questions.prompt: For the matrix `[[5, 1], [2, 3]]`, what are TN, FP, FN and TP?
questions.explanation: Top-left is TN, top-right FP, bottom-left FN, bottom-right TP. Swapping FP and FN is the standard slip, and it comes from reading the matrix column-first.

questions.prompt: Give the position of each of TN, FP, FN and TP in a 2×2 confusion matrix.
questions.answer:
```
[[TN, FP],
 [FN, TP]]
```

**TN** top-left — actually 0, predicted 0.
**FP** top-right — actually 0, predicted 1.
**FN** bottom-left — actually 1, predicted 0.
**TP** bottom-right — actually 1, predicted 1.

The diagonal is correct; the off-diagonal is the two kinds of mistake.

questions.prompt: A perfect classifier's confusion matrix has what shape?
questions.explanation: The slide shows `array([[54579, 0], [0, 5421]])` for perfect predictions — every off-diagonal entry is zero.

questions.prompt: In a spam detector, what is a false positive?
options: A legitimate email marked as spam
A spam email that reached the inbox
questions.explanation: Positive = the thing being detected (spam). False positive = wrongly flagged. This is usually the more costly error for a spam filter.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a positive example the classifier failed to detect?
A confusion matrix reads `[[{{tn}}, {{fp}}], [{{fn}}, {{tp}}]]`. How many examples were evaluated in total?

steps.text: Every example lands in exactly one of the four cells.

questions.prompt: A confusion matrix reads `[[{{100 - tp - fp - fn}}, {{fp}}], [{{fn}}, {{tp}}]]`. Give the accuracy.

steps.text: Accuracy is the diagonal over the total: `(TN + TP) / (TN + FP + FN + TP)`.
The four cells sum to 100, and the two mistakes are `{{fp}} + {{fn}} = {{fp + fn}}`.

questions.explanation: Out of 100 examples, accuracy is just "100 minus the off-diagonal". Worth remembering how little that says on its own: c4's 5-detector reaches ~91% accuracy while catching no 5s at all.

questions.prompt: A confusion matrix reads `[[{{tn}}, {{fp}}], [{{fn}}, {{tp}}]]`. How many examples were **actually** positive?

steps.text: Actual classes are **rows**, so the positives are the whole bottom row.

questions.explanation: Row for actual, column for predicted. Reading down the last column instead gives FP + TP — the number *predicted* positive, which is a different quantity.

questions.prompt: A confusion matrix reads `[[{{tn}}, {{fp}}], [{{fn}}, {{tp}}]]`. How many examples were **predicted** positive?

steps.text: Predictions are **columns**, so this is the right-hand column.

questions.prompt: Which call builds a confusion matrix in scikit-learn?
questions.explanation: True labels first, predictions second. Swapping them transposes the matrix, silently exchanging FP and FN.

questions.prompt: Why should the predictions fed to a confusion matrix come from `cross_val_predict` rather than from predicting on the training set?
questions.answer: Because a model evaluated on data it **trained on** will look far better than it is. Every prediction from `cross_val_predict` comes from a model that did **not** see that example, so the resulting matrix reflects genuine out-of-sample behaviour.

questions.prompt: The handwriting figure in c4 is described as which classifier?
options: A '5' detector — a binary classifier for the digit 5

questions.prompt: Which two cells of a 2×2 confusion matrix hold the correct predictions?
A '5 detector' on MNIST sees about 9% positives. Why is a confusion matrix more informative than accuracy here?
questions.answer:
Because a classifier that predicts 'not 5' for **everything** achieves about **91% accuracy** while catching not a single 5.

The confusion matrix exposes that immediately: TP would be 0 and FN would be the entire positive class. Accuracy alone conceals it.

subtopics.title: Precision, recall and F1
subtopics.summary: Two complementary questions, and the harmonic mean that combines them. Which denominator goes with which is the thing to get right.

formulas.name: F1 score
formulas.note: The harmonic mean of precision and recall. Low if either one is low.

formulas.name: F-beta score
formulas.note: β is how much more important recall is than precision. β = 1 gives F1.

questions.prompt: Define precision, in words and as a formula.
questions.answer:
**In words:** of the examples predicted positive, how many really are positive. For the 5-detector: 'how many of the predicted 5s are really 5s'.

**Formula:** `precision = TP / (TP + FP)`

questions.prompt: Define recall, in words and as a formula.
questions.answer:
**In words:** of the examples that really are positive, how many did we find. For the 5-detector: 'how many of the real 5s do we actually find'.

**Formula:** `recall = TP / (TP + FN)`

questions.prompt: Which metric has FP in its denominator?
questions.explanation: Precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN). Precision is punished by false alarms; recall is punished by misses.

questions.prompt: A confusion matrix reads `[[{{tn}}, {{fp}}], [{{fn}}, {{fp * mult}}]]`. Give the precision.

steps.text: Rows are actual, columns predicted, so `TP = {{tp}}` (bottom right) and `FP = {{fp}}` (top right).

questions.explanation: Of everything flagged positive, how much really was. The denominator is the whole **right-hand column** of the matrix.

questions.prompt: A confusion matrix reads `[[{{tn}}, {{fp}}], [{{fn}}, {{fn * mult}}]]`. Give the recall.
questions.explanation: Of everything that really was positive, how much we found. The denominator is the whole **bottom row** — which is why recall and precision have different denominators from the same matrix.

questions.prompt: A confusion matrix reads `[[{{tn}}, {{fp}}], [{{s - fp}}, {{(s/2) * mult}}]]`. Give the F1 score.

steps.text: Use the TP form: `F1 = TP / (TP + (FN + FP)/2)`.
`FN + FP = {{fn}} + {{fp}} = {{s}}`, so half of it is `{{half}}`.

questions.explanation: The `TP / (TP + (FN+FP)/2)` form is the one to use on paper — it avoids computing precision and recall separately and then taking a harmonic mean.

questions.prompt: A classifier has precision {{p}} and recall {{same * p + (1 - same) * (1 - p)}}. Give the F1 score.

derived.f: 2 * p * (same * p + (1 - same) * (1 - p)) / (p + (same * p + (1 - same) * (1 - p)))

questions.explanation: F1 is the **harmonic** mean, so it sits nearer the smaller of the two. Precision 1.0 with recall 0.02 averages to 0.51 arithmetically but gives an F1 of about 0.039 — which is the honest verdict.

questions.prompt: Why is F1 the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean?
questions.answer:
The harmonic mean is **dominated by the smaller value**, so F1 is only high when **both** precision and recall are high.

A classifier with precision 1.0 and recall 0.02 has an arithmetic mean of 0.51 — misleadingly respectable — but an F1 of about 0.039, which correctly reports it as useless.

questions.prompt: In the F_β score, what does β represent?
options: How much more important recall is than precision
How much more important precision is than recall
questions.explanation: The slide states it directly. β = 1 gives F1, weighting them equally; β = 2 weights recall more.

questions.prompt: Using c4's example matrix `[[5, 1], [2, 3]]` — so TP = 3, FP = 1, FN = 2 — give the F_β score for β = {{b}}.

steps.text: `1 + β² = {{1 + b^2}}`, so the numerator is `{{1 + b^2}} × 3 = {{num}}`.

questions.explanation: β weights how much more important **recall** is than precision. β = 1 is plain F1; β = 2 leans on recall, so the two false negatives in this matrix hurt more and the score drops.

questions.prompt: In a classification report, what is the difference between the macro average and the weighted average?
questions.answer:
**Macro average** — the **simple mean** across classes. Every class counts equally, however rare.

**Weighted average** — the mean **weighted by the number of samples** in each class. Large classes dominate.

The example shows this starkly: precision 1.00 and 0.10 give a macro average of 0.55 but a weighted average of 0.95, because the 1.00 class has 9485 samples against 515.

questions.prompt: In `classification_report` output, what does the 'support' column give?
options: The number of samples in that class
questions.explanation: It is what the weighted average weights by — 9485 and 515 in the example.

questions.prompt: Why can precision and recall not usually be maximised at the same time?
questions.answer:
They are traded against each other by the **decision threshold**.

Raising the threshold means predicting positive only when confident: fewer false positives, so **precision rises**, but more missed positives, so **recall falls**. Lowering it does the reverse.

One knob moves both, in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: How could a classifier trivially achieve precision of 1.0, and why is that not useful?
questions.answer:
By predicting positive **only for the single example it is most confident about**. If that one is right, FP = 0 and precision is 1.0.

It is useless because **recall would be almost zero** — every other positive is missed. This is exactly why the two are always reported together, and why F1 punishes it.

questions.prompt: precision = TP / (TP + {{1}}) and recall = TP / (TP + {{2}}).
The worked MNIST example gives precision 0.7326, recall 0.8019 and F1 0.7657. What does the relationship between the three show?
options: F1 lies between precision and recall, nearer the smaller one
F1 is the arithmetic mean of the two
F1 is unrelated to the other two
questions.explanation: The arithmetic mean would be 0.7673; F1 is 0.7657 — slightly lower, pulled toward the smaller value. That gap is the harmonic mean at work.

subtopics.title: Thresholds and precision-recall curves
subtopics.summary: A classifier returns a score, not a class. Choosing where to cut that score is a separate decision, and the precision-recall curve shows every choice at once.

questions.prompt: What does a classifier actually return before a class is decided, and how is the class obtained?
questions.answer:
A **numeric score** from `decision_function`.

The class comes from comparing that score to a **threshold**: `y_pred = (y_scores > threshold)`. The default threshold is 0, but nothing forces that choice — moving it trades precision against recall.

questions.prompt: Raising the decision threshold has what effect?
options: Precision goes up, recall goes down
Precision goes down, recall goes up
questions.explanation: A higher bar means fewer positive predictions: fewer false alarms (precision up) but more misses (recall down).

questions.prompt: The digit-strip figure shows precision 6/8 = 75% with recall 6/6 = 100% at one threshold, and precision 3/3 = 100% with recall 3/6 = 50% at another. What does it demonstrate?
options: Moving the threshold right raises precision and lowers recall
Precision and recall always move together
Accuracy is a better metric here
questions.explanation: Three thresholds along one score axis, with the middle at 4/5 = 80% precision and 4/6 = 67% recall. One knob, two metrics moving oppositely.

questions.prompt: At a chosen threshold, {{den}} examples are predicted positive and {{den * f}} of them really are. Give the precision.

steps.text: Precision counts only what was predicted positive: `{{den * f}} / {{den}}`.

questions.explanation: This is what the digit-strip figure does at each threshold: count the predicted-positive group, then count how many of them are really 5s — 6/8 = 75%, then 4/5 = 80%, then 3/3 = 100%.

questions.prompt: There are {{den}} actual positives, and at this threshold the classifier finds {{den * f}} of them. Give the recall.

steps.text: Recall counts against the actual positives: `{{den * f}} / {{den}}`.

questions.explanation: The denominator never moves as the threshold changes — the number of real positives is fixed — so recall only ever falls as the threshold rises. In the strip figure it goes 6/6 = 100%, 4/6 = 67%, 3/6 = 50%.

questions.prompt: How are out-of-sample scores obtained for plotting a precision-recall curve?
questions.explanation: Without `method="decision_function"` you get hard labels, and a curve built from labels has only one point.

questions.prompt: What does `precision_recall_curve(y_train_5, y_scores)` return?
options: Arrays of precisions, recalls and thresholds
A single precision and recall pair

questions.prompt: On the precision-and-recall-versus-threshold plot, how do the two lines behave as the threshold increases?
options: Precision rises toward 1 while recall falls toward 0
questions.explanation: They cross around 0.8 near threshold 0 in the figure. Precision is the rising dashed line; recall the falling solid one.

questions.prompt: `precisions`, `recalls` and `thresholds` come from `precision_recall_curve`. Explain what `thresholds[np.argmax(precisions >= 0.90)]` computes.
questions.answer:
`precisions >= 0.90` is a boolean array. `np.argmax` returns the index of the **first True**, since True counts as 1 — so this finds the **lowest threshold that still achieves 90% precision**.

Indexing `thresholds` with it gives that threshold. Applying it yields precision exactly 0.9 and recall about 0.599 — the price paid in recall for the precision demanded.

questions.prompt: On the precision-recall curve, what is on each axis?
options: Recall on x, precision on y
Precision on x, recall on y
Threshold on x, precision on y
FPR on x, TPR on y
questions.explanation: `plt.plot(recall, precision, 'b-')`. The last option describes the ROC curve instead.

questions.prompt: What shape does a good precision-recall curve have?
options: High precision maintained as recall increases, dropping sharply only near recall 1
Rising steadily from left to right
questions.explanation: The figure holds near 1.0 precision to about 0.4 recall, then declines, collapsing beyond 0.9.

questions.prompt: A medical screening test and a spam filter need different thresholds. Explain which way each should go.
questions.answer:
**Medical screening** — a missed case is far worse than a false alarm, so favour **recall**: use a **low** threshold and accept more false positives.

**Spam filter** — deleting a real email is worse than letting spam through, so favour **precision**: use a **high** threshold and accept more misses.

The threshold encodes the relative cost of the two error types, which is a domain decision rather than a modelling one.

questions.prompt: With `threshold = 0`, the expression `y_scores > threshold` returns `array([False])` for a decision-function score of −45148. What does that mean?
options: The score is far below the threshold, so it is classified negative
The classifier failed to produce a score
The example is a true positive
questions.explanation: The decision function returns a signed distance from the boundary, and this one sits a long way on the negative side. Lowering the threshold far enough would flip it to positive.

questions.prompt: A classifier's `decision_function` returns scores running to ±1,600,000. Does the scale matter?
questions.answer:
No. Only the **ordering** matters, and where the threshold is placed relative to it. The scores are unnormalised distances from the decision boundary, not probabilities.

This is why thresholds are chosen from the data via `precision_recall_curve` rather than picked as round numbers.

questions.prompt: Lowering the decision threshold {{1}} recall and {{2}} precision.

subtopics.title: ROC and AUC
subtopics.summary: The other threshold-free view: true positive rate against false positive rate. AUC summarises it in one number that needs no threshold and copes with imbalance.

keyFacts.definition: True positive rate (TPR) plotted against false positive rate (FPR) for all possible thresholds. Best at (0,1); the diagonal is a random classifier.
Area under the ROC curve. **1.0** for the best possible classifier, **0.5** for random. Very popular: needs no threshold and works well for imbalanced data.

questions.prompt: What does an ROC curve plot, and where are its landmark points?
questions.answer:
**True positive rate (TPR)** on the y-axis against **false positive rate (FPR)** on the x-axis, for **all possible thresholds**.

**Best** is the top-left corner, **(0, 1)** — everything found, nothing falsely flagged.
The **diagonal** is a random classifier.

questions.prompt: What are the AUC values for a perfect and for a random classifier, and why is AUC popular?
questions.answer:
**1.0** for the best possible classifier, **0.5** for a random one.

Popular because it **does not need a threshold** — it summarises performance across all of them — and it **works well for imbalanced data**.

questions.prompt: An AUC of 0.5 means:
options: The classifier is no better than random
The threshold is set at the median score

questions.prompt: An ROC curve comes out as a single sharp corner rather than a smooth arc. What has gone wrong?
questions.answer:
**`y_pred` was passed instead of `y_score`.**

Hard labels take only two values, so there is only one threshold to sweep and the curve degenerates to a corner. `roc_curve` needs the continuous scores from `decision_function`.

The course flags this explicitly as a common mistake.

questions.prompt: The 'Common mistake' slide shows an angular ROC curve. What causes it?
options: Using accuracy as the scoring metric

questions.prompt: Which call produces the values for an ROC plot?
In `plot_roc_curve`, what does `plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--')` draw?
options: The dashed diagonal representing a random classifier

questions.prompt: The true positive rate is the same quantity as which other metric?
questions.explanation: TPR = TP/(TP+FN), which is recall. The ROC curve therefore plots recall against the false alarm rate.

questions.prompt: At a given threshold, TP = {{fn * mult}} and FN = {{fn}}. Give the true positive rate.

steps.text: TPR is another name for **recall**: `TP / (TP + FN)`.

questions.prompt: At a given threshold, FP = {{fp}} and TN = {{fp * mult}}. Give the false positive rate.

steps.text: FPR is the share of **actual negatives** wrongly flagged: `FP / (FP + TN)`.

questions.explanation: The ROC curve plots TPR against this. Note that FPR uses the **top row** of the matrix, so it is unaffected by how many positives exist — which is why ROC can look flattering on very imbalanced data.

questions.prompt: The worked example gives `roc_auc_score(y_train_5, y_scores)` = 0.9585. How should that be read?
options: A strong classifier — well above the 0.5 random baseline

questions.prompt: Why does AUC handle imbalanced data better than accuracy?
questions.answer:
Accuracy is dominated by the majority class: with 91% negatives, predicting 'negative' always scores 91% while catching nothing.

AUC is built from **TPR and FPR**, each normalised **within its own class** — TPR by the actual positives, FPR by the actual negatives. Class sizes cancel out, so the majority class cannot carry the score.

questions.prompt: What do the ROC curve and the precision-recall curve have in common, and how do they differ?
questions.answer:
**In common:** both describe a classifier across **all thresholds** rather than at one, and both are built from the same score array.

**Differ:** ROC plots **TPR against FPR**, so both axes are normalised within a class. PR plots **precision against recall**, and precision depends on the ratio of positives to negatives — so the PR curve is more sensitive to class imbalance, and often more informative when positives are rare.

questions.prompt: At which coordinate is an ROC curve best?
Which of these can be computed **without** first choosing a decision threshold?
questions.explanation: Precision, recall and F1 all need hard predictions, which need a threshold. AUC integrates over all of them — the property the slide highlights.

subtopics.title: Multi-class, multilabel and multioutput
subtopics.summary: Three different generalisations beyond binary. OvR and OvO turn binary classifiers into multi-class ones; multilabel allows several binary targets; multioutput allows several multiclass targets.

keyFacts.definition: **Macro** — compute F1 for each label separately, then average over labels. **Micro** — compute F1 for the labels per example, then average over examples.

questions.prompt: OneVsOneClassifier is used on a problem with {{n}} classes. How many binary estimators does it train?

steps.text: One-vs-One trains a classifier for every **pair** of classes.
The number of pairs from n classes is `n(n − 1)/2 = {{n}} × {{n - 1}} / 2`.

questions.explanation: With 10 classes this gives 45, matching `len(ovo_clf.estimators_)` in the example.

questions.prompt: A one-versus-one classifier reports 45 fitted estimators. How many classes does the problem have?
questions.explanation: n(n−1)/2 = 45 gives n = 10 — the ten MNIST digits.

questions.prompt: One-vs-Rest is used on a problem with {{n}} classes. How many binary classifiers are trained?

steps.text: One-vs-Rest trains one classifier per class: that class against everything else.
So the count is simply the number of classes.

questions.explanation: Far fewer than OvO's n(n−1)/2, though each is trained on the full dataset rather than on two classes' worth.

questions.prompt: Explain how `np.argmax(some_digit_scores)` combined with `sgd_clf.classes_` produces a prediction.
questions.answer:
`decision_function` returns one score per class. `np.argmax` gives the **index** of the highest — 5 in the example.

`classes_` maps indices back to labels: `array([0,1,…,9])`, so `classes_[5]` is 5.

The index and the label coincide here only because the classes are the digits 0–9 in order. In general you **must** go through `classes_`.

questions.prompt: What is multilabel classification?
options: More than one binary target per example
More than two classes for a single target
questions.explanation: The example builds `y_multilabel = np.c_[y_train_large, y_train_odd]` — is the digit ≥ 7, and is it odd. Two independent yes/no questions about one image.

questions.prompt: Describe the multilabel example and what the classifier returns.
questions.answer:
Two binary targets are built for each digit image:
- `y_train_large = (y_train >= 7)`
- `y_train_odd = (y_train % 2 == 1)`
stacked as `y_multilabel = np.c_[y_train_large, y_train_odd]`.

A `KNeighborsClassifier` fitted on this returns **two booleans per instance**: `array([[False, True]])` — not large, but odd. The digit 5 fits exactly.

questions.prompt: Distinguish macro from micro averaging for multilabel F1.
questions.answer:
**Macro** — compute F1 for **each label separately**, then average over all labels. Every label counts equally.

**Micro** — compute F1 for **the labels per example**, then average over all examples.

Macro treats labels as the unit; micro treats examples as the unit.

questions.prompt: In the error analysis, why is `np.fill_diagonal(norm_conf_mx, 0)` applied before plotting?
questions.answer:
The diagonal holds the **correct** predictions, which are much larger than everything else. Displayed as an image, the diagonal saturates white and the errors are invisible.

Zeroing it rescales the display so the **off-diagonal confusions** become readable — which is the point of error analysis. The white in the first plot is about 10000; in the second, about 500.
